readerTitle: A product for everyone is a product for no one
caseNote: 가상 사례 (같은 거리의 두 빵집, 예약 소프트웨어) + 용어의 기원 (Wendell Smith, 1956)
insight: 고객 세그먼트는 나이나 성별 같은 꼬리표가 아니라, 우리가 다르게 행동해야 하는 고객 집단이다. 나눴는데 할 일이 바뀌지 않으면 세그먼트가 아니다.
misconception: 모두를 위한 제품이 가장 많은 고객을 모은다. 고객을 나누는 것은 나이, 성별, 회사 규모로 나누는 것이다.

sources.text: Smith, W. R. (1956). Product Differentiation and Market Segmentation as Alternative Marketing Strategies. Journal of Marketing, 21(1), 3–8.
빵집과 예약 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Wendell Smith(1956)의 Journal of Marketing 논문이 '시장 세분화(market segmentation)' 개념을 널리 알린 초기 문헌이라는 점을 게시 전에 확인하세요. 카드에는 '최초로 만들었다'가 아니라 'helped popularize'로 적었습니다.
빵집, 예약 앱 사례는 모두 가상이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다. 카드에 illustrative 표시를 붙였습니다.

cards.title: A product for everyone is a product for no one
body: Two bakeries sit on the same street. Same ovens, same flour, similar prices.
The first tries to have something for everyone: forty items, open all day. The second decided it serves two kinds of customers, and built around them. A year later, only one of them is busy.

image.label: Two bakeries side by side on one street
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 같은 거리에 나란히 선 빵집 두 곳. 왼쪽은 진열대가 빽빽하고 손님이 드문드문, 오른쪽은 아침 출근객이 빠르게 줄을 서 있고 창문에 'Cake pre-orders' 안내. 실제 브랜드 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run the first bakery. Sales are flat.
body: Your regulars include commuters grabbing breakfast at 7am, families ordering birthday cakes for the weekend, and students who linger in the afternoon.

options.text: Add more items so every visitor finds something they like
options.feedback: More choice feels generous, but a longer menu slows the morning line and still doesn't make you the go-to place for cakes.

options.text: Notice which groups want different things, and change how you serve each
options.feedback: You give up being equally fine for everyone. In return, you become clearly better for the groups that matter most.

options.text: Find your largest age group and aim your marketing at them
options.feedback: Looking at who buys is a good start. But a 25-year-old and a 60-year-old commuter want the same thing: speed.

cards.title: The second bakery saw two different jobs.
body: Its owner noticed that morning customers wanted **speed**, while cake customers wanted **certainty**: the right cake, ready on time.
So mornings got a short grab-and-go counter with coffee and five pastries. Cakes moved to an order-ahead form with pickup slots.
Each change made one group much happier and cost the other almost nothing. The first bakery kept adding items. Its mornings got slower, and the cake orders went down the street.

cards.title: Customer segments
body: A **customer segment** is a group of customers who want something different from other groups, so you need to act differently to serve them.
The test is simple. If two groups would want the same product, price, hours and service from you, they are one segment. If serving them well means doing different things, they are two.

image.label: One crowd sorted into two groups by what they need
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 섞여 있는 사람들, 가운데 깔때기, 오른쪽에 두 그룹: 'Needs speed'(커피 컵, 시계 아이콘)와 'Needs certainty'(케이크 상자, 달력 아이콘). 나이나 성별로 나누지 않는다는 점이 보이도록 각 그룹 안 인물의 나이와 모습을 다양하게.

cards.title: Sort by need and situation, not by label.
body: The idea is old. Marketer Wendell Smith helped popularize market segmentation in a 1956 paper. The useful part is how you draw the lines. Ask:
list: **What are they trying to get done?** A quick breakfast or a perfect cake
**When and how do they buy?** Walk-in, or planned days ahead
**What would make them switch?** A slow line, or a late cake
cards.callout: The same person can be in two segments: a commuter on Monday, a cake buyer on Saturday.

cards.title: Segments shape the whole business.
body: Segments are not only about who sees your ads. They decide your opening hours, your product range, your prices and how people order.

A hotel may serve business travelers who value a fast check-in and weekend couples who value a late checkout. Same rooms, different promises. Treat them as one crowd and you deliver a promise neither group cares about.
cards.softwareNote: In software, segments often show up in usage data. Two groups of users may sign up for the same product but use completely different features, and they often churn for different reasons.

cards.title: More segments is not always better.
body: Each segment you serve separately costs something: extra staff, extra products, extra decisions. A segment is only worth it if it is big enough to pay for that, you can reach it, and you can actually serve it differently.
Some segments also pull against each other. Lingering students and rushed commuters can clash at the same counter. Sometimes the right choice is to serve one group well and let the other go.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app.
body: Your appointment app is sold to "small businesses." Sign-ups come from hair salons, dental clinics and yoga studios. Salons ask for deposits to stop no-shows. Clinics ask for patient forms and privacy. Studios ask for class passes. Your roadmap is jammed.

options.text: Build all the requests as settings, so every business can turn on what it needs
options.feedback: Everyone gets a little, slowly. The product grows complex, and no group gets a tool clearly built for it.

options.text: Group sign-ups by what they need and how they pay, then serve one group deeply first
options.feedback: You say "not yet" to some users. In return, one segment gets a product that fits so well they recommend it.

options.text: Split customers into small, medium and large businesses
options.feedback: Size is easy to measure, but a small salon and a small clinic still need very different things from you.

cards.title: Group customers by what they need you to do differently.
body: If a way of grouping customers doesn't change what you'd do, it isn't a useful segment.
**Try it today:** list your last ten customers. Next to each, write what they were trying to get done. How many different groups do you see, and are you serving each one on purpose?
